explanations.explanation: That's it, friend. Jairus, a synagogue leader, falls at Jesus' feet and begs, and the text gives the reason: “…his only daughter, who was about twelve, was dying.” (Luke 8:42) A man in his position drops to the ground in front of everybody. I think that tells you how much he needed Jesus to come.

explanations.answer: His only son has a fever
explanations.explanation: Close on the "only child" part, but this one is a daughter, not a son. Luke says Jairus came because “…his only daughter, who was about twelve, was dying.” (Luke 8:42) And it's more serious than a fever, since she's dying. Keep that in mind, because the rest of the story leans on it.

You might be thinking of a different story, since Jesus does help a centurion's paralyzed servant in Matthew 8:5-6. But Jairus is not asking for a servant. The text says he begs Jesus to come because “…his only daughter, who was about twelve, was dying.” (Luke 8:42) This one is about a father and his little girl.

Twelve it is. Luke says the girl "was about twelve," so the text gives us a rough age, not an exact one. Jairus' only daughter is right on the edge of growing up. I think that makes his begging hit even harder.
Seven is a good Bible number, but it's not the one here. The text says his only daughter "was about twelve." (Luke 8:42) So she's older than seven. Think of a girl just about to be grown.
Good guess, but she's a little younger than that. Luke says she "was about twelve." (Luke 8:42) Notice he says "about," so even the text isn't giving a birthday. Four years off is a big gap, friend!

Yes, physicians. Luke says she "had spent all her money on physicians." (Luke 8:43) That's every last coin, handed over to doctors in hope of getting better. I think she was running out of places to turn.

Sacrifices were a real part of life back then, but Luke doesn't mention them here. He says she "had spent all her money on physicians." (Luke 8:43) So her money went to doctors. That's the only place the text says it went.
A long trip is a fair guess, but it isn't in the text. Luke says she "had spent all her money on physicians." (Luke 8:43) She spent every bit of it on doctors. No travel plans in this story, friend.

Not quite. Luke says she "had spent all her money on physicians, but no one was able to heal her." (Luke 8:43) So she paid every doctor and none of them could do it. The healing is still coming, and it doesn't come from the doctors.

Right. The text says she "had spent all her money on physicians, but no one was able to heal her." (Luke 8:43) Twelve years, all her money, and still no healing. So whatever happens next, it won't come from the doctors.
That's the one. She "came up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of His cloak." (Luke 8:44) Not a grab, not a tug, just the edge of it. Small touch, and a very big moment.

Down by His feet is a fair guess, but Luke doesn't say that. The woman "came up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of His cloak." (Luke 8:44) So it's the edge of His cloak. She never goes anywhere near His sandals.

That's a creative one, friend, but the text doesn't mention a sash. She "came up behind Jesus and touched the fringe of His cloak." (Luke 8:44) It's just the edge of the cloak, reached from behind in a pushing crowd. No sash in this scene.
Immediately, baker! The text says she touched the fringe and "immediately her bleeding stopped." (Luke 8:44) No waiting around and no slow improvement. After twelve years, it stopped on the spot.

Overnight would still be pretty quick, but the text is faster. It says "immediately her bleeding stopped." (Luke 8:44) She didn't have to sleep on it or wait for morning. It happened the moment she touched Him.

Gradual healing is how most things go, like a dough that takes its sweet time to rise. But Luke says "immediately her bleeding stopped." (Luke 8:44) No slow improvement. It was right there, right then.
Yep. When Jesus asks "Who touched Me?" the text says, "they all denied it." (Luke 8:45) Everybody in that crowd says it wasn't them. Nobody has stepped forward yet.

explanations.answer: They all point at the woman
explanations.explanation: Nobody points at her in the text. Luke says that after Jesus asks, "they all denied it." (Luke 8:45) She is still hiding in the crowd at this point. The crowd is just saying it wasn't them.

The text doesn't have anyone blaming anybody. After Jesus asks who touched Him, "they all denied it." (Luke 8:45) Then Peter, one of Jesus' disciples, speaks up about the crowd pressing against Jesus. That's a comment about the crowd, not a pointing finger.

explanations.answer: Power has gone out from Him
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus says, "Someone touched Me, for I know that power has gone out from Me." (Luke 8:46) He knows this from what He felt go out of Him, not from the crowd's shoving. Lots of people bump into Him, but only one touch carries that.

explanations.answer: He saw her reach for His cloak
explanations.explanation: The text never says He saw her. She came "up behind" Him, and later Luke says she "could not escape notice." (Luke 8:44, 47) What Jesus gives as His reason is this: "…I know that power has gone out from Me." (Luke 8:46) That's how He knows.

explanations.answer: Peter pointed her out to Him
explanations.explanation: Peter does speak up, but not to point her out. He says, "…the people are crowding and pressing against You." (Luke 8:45) Jesus' reason is different: "…I know that power has gone out from Me." (Luke 8:46) Peter's comment was about the crowd.

True. Luke says that "in the presence of all the people, she explained why she had touched Him and how she had immediately been healed." (Luke 8:47) She went from hiding to telling the whole crowd. I think that took everything she had.

Actually, she does explain. Luke says that "in the presence of all the people, she explained why she had touched Him and how she had immediately been healed." (Luke 8:47) She didn't slip away. She told her story right in front of everybody.
Her faith, baker. Jesus says, "Daughter, your faith has healed you. Go in peace." (Luke 8:48) He names it plainly. Twelve years of no answers, and He sends her off with this.

Luke says she came trembling, but tears aren't what Jesus names. He says, "Daughter, your faith has healed you." (Luke 8:48) So faith is what He points to. Tears don't come up in this part of the story.
I think it took plenty of courage to step out in front of that crowd. But that isn't the word Jesus uses. He says, "Daughter, your faith has healed you. Go in peace." (Luke 8:48) Faith is the answer.
Yes. The messenger tells Jairus, "Your daughter is dead." (Luke 8:49) This is a heavy moment. I think this one hurts, so let's give it room.
This part of the story goes the other way. The messenger says, "Your daughter is dead." (Luke 8:49) It's a heavy turn, and I think it hurts. Stay with it, because Jesus isn't done yet.

The messenger's news is about the girl, not Jairus' wife. He says, "Your daughter is dead." (Luke 8:49) It's the hardest news Jairus could hear. I think this is the part of the story that hurts the most.

No, it goes the opposite direction. The messenger tells Jairus, "Your daughter is dead. Do not bother the Teacher anymore." (Luke 8:49) So it's a message to stop, not hurry. Jesus is the one who steps in next.

Right. The messenger tells Jairus, "Your daughter is dead. Do not bother the Teacher anymore." (Luke 8:49) There's no hurry in it, only a stop sign. But Jesus overhears, and He has something different to say.

explanations.answer: Don't be afraid and just believe
explanations.explanation: That's it. Jesus overhears and tells Jairus, "Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed." (Luke 8:50) He says it right after the news that the girl is dead. Jairus doesn't have to carry that alone.

explanations.answer: Go home and comfort your wife
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't send Jairus away. He says, "Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed." (Luke 8:50) Then He goes on toward the house with him. The text never mentions Jairus' wife at this point.

explanations.answer: Wait here while I pray for her
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't tell him to wait. He says, "Do not be afraid; just believe, and she will be healed." (Luke 8:50) Then He keeps going toward the house. Luke doesn't have Him stop to pray here.

Not this crowd. Luke says that when Jesus entered the house, "He did not allow anyone to go in with Him except Peter, John, James, and the child's father and mother." (Luke 8:51) Only a small few get to go in with Him. The rest stay outside.

Correct. Luke says that when Jesus entered the house, "He did not allow anyone to go in with Him except Peter, John, James, and the child's father and mother." (Luke 8:51) It's a very short list. Think of a packed room that suddenly gets quiet.
Mother, yes. Jesus allows only Peter, John, James, "and the child's father and mother." (Luke 8:51) So both of her parents are in the room. Peter, John and James are three of His disciples.

A brother isn't on the list. The text says Jesus allowed in only Peter, John, James, "and the child's father and mother." (Luke 8:51) That makes five people with Jesus in the room. The text names no brother for her.

That's a thoughtful guess, but no nurse is named. Luke says Jesus allowed in only Peter, John, James, "and the child's father and mother." (Luke 8:51) So her parents are the ones in the room. Peter, John and James are three of His disciples.

explanations.answer: She is not dead but asleep
explanations.explanation: Right. While everyone is weeping and mourning, Jesus says, "Stop weeping; she is not dead but asleep." (Luke 8:52) It's a surprising thing to say in that room. Keep reading, because the next verses show what He means.

Jesus says something different, and bigger. He tells them, "Stop weeping; she is not dead but asleep." (Luke 8:52) He's speaking to a room full of people who are mourning. Sick isn't the word He uses.

explanations.answer: She will wake in three days
explanations.explanation: Jesus doesn't give a timeline here. He says, "Stop weeping; she is not dead but asleep." (Luke 8:52) No days are mentioned in this passage. Her waking comes very soon, as you'll see.
Yes. Luke says, "And they laughed at Him, knowing that she was dead." (Luke 8:53) They knew she was dead, so His words made no sense to them. Jesus keeps going anyway.
No shouting is recorded here. Luke says, "And they laughed at Him, knowing that she was dead." (Luke 8:53) They knew what they had seen. So Jesus' words sounded laughable to them.

Staring is a fair guess, but the text gives a stronger reaction. It says, "And they laughed at Him, knowing that she was dead." (Luke 8:53) They were sure of what they knew. They laughed at what Jesus said.
That's it. Jesus takes her by the hand and calls out, "Child, get up!" (Luke 8:54) Simple words, spoken while holding her hand. Next comes the part everyone in that room could not believe.
Reasonable guess, but those aren't His words. Luke says Jesus took her by the hand and called out, "Child, get up!" (Luke 8:54) It's a short command, with her hand in His.
I can see why you'd guess that, but it's not what the text says. Jesus took her by the hand and called out, "Child, get up!" (Luke 8:54) Just those words, with no speech around them.
True. Luke says, "Her spirit returned, and at once she got up." (Luke 8:55) No delay at all. Jesus called, and she got up.
Actually, she does. Luke says, "Her spirit returned, and at once she got up." (Luke 8:55) It happens right away. Jesus called, and she got up.
Yes. Luke says Jesus "directed that she be given something to eat." (Luke 8:55) She has just gotten up, and Jesus thinks of her next need. I think that's about as caring as it gets.

explanations.answer: Let her rest for a while
explanations.explanation: Rest is a natural guess, but the text gives a different instruction. Luke says Jesus "directed that she be given something to eat." (Luke 8:55) It's something practical and close at hand. Nothing about rest is mentioned.

Her father is a synagogue leader, so I see why you'd guess it. But Luke says Jesus "directed that she be given something to eat." (Luke 8:55) The instruction is about food. Nothing about the synagogue comes up here.
It's the opposite. Luke says that Jesus "ordered them not to tell anyone what had happened." (Luke 8:56) So the parents are told to keep quiet. The text doesn't say why.

Right. Luke says that her parents were astounded, "but Jesus ordered them not to tell anyone what had happened." (Luke 8:56) The instruction is to keep quiet. The text doesn't give a reason, so we won't guess one.
